Revised assessment using the SLOOS as context:
- Credit supply to businesses looks supportive: banks eased standards for C&I loans, cited improved economic outlook/competition/risk tolerance/liquidity/capital positions, and reported stronger loan demand across large, middle-market, and small firms with increased credit line inquiries. Banks expect improvement in business lending (non-syndicated C&I and non-leveraged syndicated) and in CRE, including construction, land development, and multifamily. This cushions growth as the Fed begins policy normalization.
- Consumer/household credit is more mixed-to-soft: banks reported weaker demand for residential real estate (including GSE and subprime) and expect deterioration in household credit quality, notably credit cards, auto (with focus on nonprime), and nonconforming jumbos. This suggests rising rates will weigh more on consumption-sensitive sectors.
- Rates backdrop: banks broadly expect higher interest rates, which should temper some demand but, given eased standards and strong business demand, does not signal an imminent credit crunch.

Net tone: compared with the FOMC statement alone, SLOOS points to more resilient near-term activity via business lending and CRE, partially offset by softer consumer credit and housing. Overall, slightly more constructive than the FSR-based read, but still cautious given inflation and geopolitical uncertainty.
